summary: Specifies an optional Content-MD5 header field for MIME messages that carries a digest of the content, so a receiver can check that the message was not corrupted. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Content-MD5 is an optional MIME header that lets a recipient check whether decoded content changed during delivery. The sender makes a digest from the content before transfer encoding, and the recipient can compare it after decoding.

questions: how to check mime message integrity
subtitle: An optional MIME field that carries a digest for checking whether content changed in transit.

tldr.problem: A recipient may want to check that decoded MIME content matches the content originally sent.
tldr.mechanism: The originating user agent computes an MD5 digest of the content in canonical form, encodes the 16-octet result with base64, and places it in Content-MD5.
tldr.outcome: The check is intended to detect accidental changes, not all deliberate modifications. RFC 1864 obsoletes RFC 1544.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1864 as a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1544. No RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating RFC 1864.

sections.title: A Check for Changed Message Content
sections.content:
MIME has mechanisms intended to protect data during email transport, but a receiver may still want to check that decoded data match what was sent. RFC 1864 defines the optional Content-MD5 header field for this purpose. The field may also be placed in the encapsulated headers of a message/external-body object to check retrieved and decoded data.

MD5 computes a 128-bit digest from data of any length. This memo specifies its use for MIME mail; it does not define the MD5 algorithm itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Content-MD5 gives a recipient a way to check whether MIME content changed in transit. It carries a short digest made from the content, not from the encoded form sent through email.

sections.title: How the Sender Makes the Field
sections.content:
Only the originating user agent generates Content-MD5. Message relays and gateways must not generate it. The field is optional and may be added only to a MIME entity that is not a multipart entity or a message/rfc822 entity.

The sender computes MD5 on the entity's canonical form, before applying content-transfer-encoding. For text, canonical newlines use a carriage return followed by a line feed. The digest is 128 bits, or 16 octets, viewed in network byte order; the sender encodes those octets with base64 for the field value. The RFC says quoted-printable or base64 transfer encoding should be used because adding or removing trailing white space changes the digest.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender's mail program makes the digest from the content in its standard form, before encoding it for delivery. It then puts the base64 version of that digest in the header.

sections.title: How the Recipient Checks the Field
sections.content:
When Content-MD5 is present, a recipient user agent may use it to check whether the MIME entity changed during transport. The recipient first undoes any content-transfer-encoding, computes MD5 on the canonical form, and can compare the result with the field value.

Relays and gateways must not change how they process a message because Content-MD5 is present. A gateway may remove the field if it translates the entity to a different content type.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient can decode the content, make the same digest, and compare the result with the header. Mail relays must not change their handling because the field is present.

sections.title: What the Integrity Check Does Not Protect
sections.content: The RFC describes Content-MD5 as protection against accidental modification while data travel from sender to recipient. It distinguishes this from a secure data-integrity service, such as the one provided by Privacy-Enhanced Mail, which it says is intended to protect against all modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Content-MD5 can help reveal accidental changes. The RFC does not present it as protection against someone deliberately changing the content.
